title: SpikeCount, two networks in a row
caption: One network outlines the red blood cells in the photo; the other looks at each cell on its own and names its shape, from normal disc to spiky ball.
alt: Architecture diagram of SpikeCount, two networks in a row. Along the bottom, left to right: a grey microscope photo of red blood cells (572 by 572 pixels); the outliner's pixel map, where each pixel is scored as background, cell interior or cell edge; three cut-out cells, one 96 by 96 crop per cell (53 crops for this photo); and the same photo with each cell the outliner found drawn in the colour of its grade, 31 of 53 cells spiky, 58.5 percent. Above them, panel (a), the outliner, a U-Net with 2.8 million parameters: the photo, standardized and padded to 576 pixels, passes a MobileNetV4-Conv-Small encoder (576 by 576 down to 18 by 18), five decoder blocks (upsample by 2, then two 3 by 3 convolutions, with skip connections from the encoder) and a 3 by 3 convolution with softmax that gives 3 classes per pixel. Each cell found in that map is then cut out of the photo as a 96 by 96 crop. Panel (b), the grader, 8.4 million parameters, runs once per cell: the crop is upsampled by 2 (bilinear) to 192 by 192, then passes a MobileNetV4-Conv-Medium backbone (down to 6 by 6 by 960), average pooling and a 1 by 1 convolution (960 to 1280), and a linear layer with softmax over 6 classes: normal disc, spiky grade 1, 2, 3 and 4, and cup-shaped. Images: held-out field 96 of the RedTell set (Sadafi et al. 2023, CC BY 4.0). AI-generated diagram.
